title: API 510 Training in Mobile, AL: Vessel Inspector Exam Prep
description: Self-paced API 510 exam prep for Mobile vessel inspectors: Saraland hydrocracker reactors, chlor-alkali equipment and Theodore columns, with instructor Q&A.
h1: API 510 Training in Mobile, Alabama: Pressure Vessel Inspector Exam Prep for the Saraland Refinery and the Mobile River Chemical Corridor
html:
API 510 exam prep for pressure vessel inspectors from Saraland to McIntosh

Drive north from downtown Mobile along the river and you pass plants holding almost every kind of pressure vessel the API 510 examination asks about: hydrocracker reactors and high-pressure separators at the Saraland refinery, columns, reactors and receivers in the specialty chemical units at Theodore, and the equipment of a chlor-alkali complex upriver at McIntosh. This page is for the people who already look after that equipment: plant inspectors, contract inspectors, NDT technicians who take the thickness readings, and reliability engineers who want API 510 certification behind their recommendations.

There is no Atlantis classroom in Mobile. The API 510 course is self-paced and online, and an instructor answers your questions while you study, so a candidate in Saraland, Chickasaw, Theodore or across the bay in Daphne works from the same material at whatever hour suits the roster. API, the American Petroleum Institute, decides who is eligible, administers the examination at Prometric test centres and certifies the inspectors who pass. The course prepares you for that examination and grants nothing itself, and Atlantis is not an API-approved training provider.

The Saraland refinery and the vessels its units imply

The U.S. Energy Information Administration's refinery capacity survey, which describes the position at the start of 2026, lists three operating refineries in Alabama. The largest is Vertex Refining Alabama LLC at Saraland, just north of Mobile, at 88,000 barrels per calendar day of crude distillation. The two others are Hunt Refining at Tuscaloosa and Goodway Refining at Atmore, the second of them small enough that a Mobile inspector may never see it. Shell sold the Saraland refinery to Vertex in 2022, together with the Blakeley Island crude and products terminal. Vertex Energy went through Chapter 11 in 2024 and came out of it as a privately held company owned by its lenders, and it still runs the refinery through the same Alabama subsidiary.

Unit listed by EIA at SaralandBarrels per stream dayVessels an inspector meets there
Vacuum distillation29,000A large-diameter column under vacuum, with hot bottoms and heavy wash zones
Gas oil hydrocracking30,000Thick-walled reactors, high-pressure separators, feed-effluent exchangers
High-pressure catalytic reforming22,000Reactors and interheater circuits in hot hydrogen, product separators
Naphtha hydrotreating26,700Reactor, separator and stripper in hydrogen and hydrogen sulfide service
Kerosene and jet hydrotreating18,000A second, smaller reactor train
Diesel hydrotreating17,000A third reactor train and its stripper

EIA lists no coker and no fluid catalytic cracker at Saraland, so the hot, erosive regenerator work that dominates some Gulf refineries is absent here. What the site does have is a lot of hydroprocessing for its size, and that is where several of the harder API 510 topics live. The hydrocracker has its own history: Vertex converted it to renewable diesel in 2023 and returned it to crude-derived feeds the following year, and in 2026 the company approved a project to make Group III base oils from the hydrocracker's vacuum gas oil stream, with a high-pressure lubricants hydrotreating unit already procured and production planned for 2029. For an inspector that means new vessels to receive, baseline and add to the inspection plan, which is API 510 work from the first day.

Chemical plants on the Mobile River corridor

The Mobile Area Chamber of Commerce describes a chemical corridor about 60 miles long, running from McIntosh in the north to Theodore in the south. Three of the names in it carry most of the vessel work.

  • Evonik, Theodore Industrial Park. Evonik began production here in 1976 and calls the site its largest manufacturing complex in North America: 28 production plants, about 750 employees and more than 250 resident contractors. Its products include coating additives for wind turbine blades, structural foams, catalysts used in biodiesel production and amino acids for animal feed. The sodium methylate plant was expanded to up to 90,000 metric tons a year in 2021, and Evonik's own photograph of that project shows a methanol recovery column.
  • Olin, McIntosh. Olin lists chlorine, caustic soda, hydrochloric acid, hydrogen, bleach and salt as products of its McIntosh plant, an industry that grew up around the area's salt domes.
  • BASF, McIntosh and Theodore. BASF makes specialty chemicals at McIntosh for its performance chemicals business. In 2026 it said several production lines there will stop by spring 2027 while the site continues at a reduced footprint; its Theodore plant is not affected.

Twenty-eight production plants on one campus is a useful picture of chemical-plant inspection: dozens of modest vessels, many in stainless or clad construction, each with its own process fluid and its own damage picture, rather than a few very large refinery reactors. A chlor-alkali complex is different again. Equipment there handles brine, wet chlorine, caustic at several strengths and hydrochloric acid, and the materials range from carbon steel through nickel alloys and titanium to lined and non-metallic construction. Knowing which items are ASME Section VIII vessels, which are something else, and how that changes your inspection plan is itself a skill the exam rewards.

Alabama law and why plant vessels sit with the owner

Alabama's Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Act is administered by the Inspection Division of the Alabama Department of Workforce, which issues operating certificates and installation permits for the equipment the Act regulates. Section 25-12-7 of the Code of Alabama then lists what the Act does not regulate, and several entries matter on this corridor:

  • boilers and pressure vessels operated and maintained as part of a manufacturing process, whose operator must be insured or self-insured;
  • boilers and pressure vessels that are subject to OSHA standards of compliance;
  • under subsection (b)(7), any pressure vessel associated with oil, natural gas and their by-products, feedstock and product manufacturing, including exploration, production, gas processing, treating, refining, chemical, pipeline, supply, storage and transportation, except for buildings or businesses subject to public utilization;
  • boilers and vessels that generate electricity, which the statute still requires to be insured or self-insured and regularly inspected by an inspector holding a certificate of competency issued by the state.

The practical result for a Saraland or Theodore inspector is that refinery and chemical plant vessels are kept safe through the owner's own mechanical integrity programme rather than a state inspection cycle. That programme answers to federal process safety rules and to the codes the owner adopts, and API 510 is usually the code adopted for in-service vessels. Section 6 then sets the inspection intervals, Section 8 governs repairs, alterations and rerating, and the inspector's judgement is recorded against them. API 510 certification is what employers on the corridor ask for; the state certificate of competency is a separate credential for the power-generation equipment the statute names.

Damage mechanisms from the Body of Knowledge that Mobile vessels illustrate

The Body of Knowledge for the API 510 examinations from late 2026 into 2027 limits questions from API RP 571 to 15 damage mechanisms. Several of them can be studied with a Mobile plant in mind:

  • High-temperature hydrogen attack and high-temperature H2/H2S corrosion. These are hydrocracker and hydrotreater mechanisms. Hydrogen alone is not enough for hydrogen attack; it takes elevated temperature and hydrogen partial pressure together, which is why RP 571 is read alongside the material and operating limits of the unit.
  • Wet H2S damage, amine stress corrosion cracking and sulfidation. Wet H2S damage covers blistering, HIC, SOHIC and sulfide stress cracking in separators and strippers downstream of hydroprocessing reactors. Amine cracking belongs to the amine systems that refineries running hydrotreaters normally have, and sulfidation to hot hydrocarbon sections such as vacuum column bottoms.
  • Caustic corrosion and caustic stress corrosion cracking. Chlor-alkali equipment and any vessel in caustic service, particularly welds that were never stress relieved.
  • Hydrochloric acid corrosion and chloride stress corrosion cracking. Acid production and recovery at McIntosh, and austenitic stainless vessels across the chemical plants.
  • Corrosion under insulation. Mobile averaged 67.1 inches of precipitation a year over 1991 to 2020, on about 117 wet days. Insulated vessels operating where moisture condenses and evaporates repeatedly, or cycling through that range, deserve the attention RP 571 gives them, and stainless vessels under wet insulation add the risk of external chloride cracking.
  • Brittle fracture. On the coast this is less about winter than about pressure testing, start-up and the minimum design metal temperature on the nameplate.

The exam does not ask about any particular plant, but candidates who can attach each mechanism to equipment they have stood beside tend to remember the critical factors, the affected materials and the inspection methods RP 571 recommends for each one.

Worked example: the bottom head of a tall column, with static head

Static head catches many candidates, and the Body of Knowledge settles one question in advance: all static head is based on a specific gravity of 1.0, which is 0.433 psi per foot. Here is a closed-book style problem of the kind a methanol or solvent column raises.

  1. The column has an inside diameter of 72 in. and an MAWP of 100 psig at the top. The question says the liquid stands 72 ft above the seam of the 2:1 ellipsoidal bottom head. Take S = 20,000 psi and E = 1.0 as given.
  2. Static head on the bottom head: 72 × 0.433 = 31.18 psi. Design pressure at that part: 100 + 31.18 = 131.18 psi.
  3. Required thickness from the ellipsoidal head formula in UG-32, t = PD ÷ (2SE − 0.2P): 131.18 × 72 = 9,444.96, and 2 × 20,000 × 1.0 − 0.2 × 131.18 = 39,973.76, so t = 0.236 in.
  4. Inspection data: the head now measures 0.312 in.; six years ago it measured 0.342 in. Corrosion rate = 0.030 ÷ 6 = 0.005 in. per year.
  5. Remaining corrosion allowance = 0.312 − 0.236 = 0.076 in. Remaining life = 0.076 ÷ 0.005 = 15.2 years.
  6. API 510 interval for internal or on-stream inspection: the lesser of half the remaining life and 10 years, so 7.6 years.

Leave the static head out and the required thickness drops to 0.180 in., the remaining life stretches to 26.4 years and the 10-year cap governs, an interval that overstates the head by more than two years. The same discipline applies to every part of a tall vessel: work out the liquid height above the part in question, add it to the pressure at the top, and only then design or evaluate that part.

Getting from a Mobile job to API 510 eligibility

API counts education and inspection experience gained in the last 10 years while employed by, or under contract with, an authorized inspection agency. The certification page sets out the detail at API 510 certification requirements; in brief, a bachelor's degree in engineering or technology needs one year of supervising or performing inspection, a two-year degree or certificate in engineering or technology needs two years, a high school diploma needs three, and no formal education needs five or more.

  • Engineers. The University of South Alabama offers a Bachelor of Science in Chemical Engineering, the shortest education route if the year that follows is spent on inspection rather than process design.
  • Process and maintenance technicians. Bishop State Community College in Mobile offers an associate degree in Process and Maintenance Technology aimed at chemical processing, utilities and steel. Whether a particular associate degree counts as engineering or technology is API's decision, so describe it accurately and be ready to fall back on the three-year route.
  • NDT technicians. Taking readings is part of inspection, but API asks about inspection activities as API 510 describes them, so the strongest applications show you evaluating results and recommending action. A supervisor can often widen your role well before you apply.
  • Welders. Repair and alteration work is relevant, but the year or years of inspection still have to be documented.

Fitting API 510 study around Mobile shifts and outage work

A self-paced course suits a corridor where rotating twelve-hour shifts, call-outs and outage weeks are normal. Most candidates do best with three phases rather than a calendar: first the codes in order of weight (API 510 itself, then the Section VIII paragraphs the Body of Knowledge names, then RP 571, 572, 576, 577 and 578, Section V, Section IX and PCC-2); then the calculations until they are routine; then timed practice papers. If your plant has an outage approaching, move the calculations and the heavy reading to the weeks before it and use the outage itself for short review of definitions and damage mechanisms. Questions that come up on the job, such as why a nozzle reinforcement looks thin or what a rerating needs, make good material for the instructor.

The open-book half rewards knowing where things are. Bookmark UG-27, UG-32, UG-99 and UW-12 in the Section VIII file, Section 7 of API 510 for corrosion rate and remaining life, and the Section V articles on the methods you use at work, because searching blind on the day costs minutes.

How Mobile candidates compare preparation routes

There are three common ways to prepare, and many candidates mix them. Seminar-style courses are held in the larger Gulf Coast cities and some people value a week away from the plant with a group. Employer study groups, where a senior inspector walks juniors through the code, are excellent for site knowledge and less consistent on the exam's open-book technique. Self-study from the codes and a question bank is cheapest in money and hardest on discipline. A self-paced online course with instructor Q&A sits between the last two: structured material and practice papers, a person to answer the questions that stall you, and no travel away from a Saraland or Theodore roster. None of these routes changes the examination, which is the same for every candidate.

Sponsoring candidates from a Mobile plant or inspection contractor

Employers can enrol several candidates at once and fees are quoted on request. Each candidate still applies to API individually, and the application is where sponsorship matters most: an inspection supervisor who confirms the dates, the equipment and the inspection duties saves weeks of back-and-forth. Contractors who staff more than one site in the corridor should keep a record of which vessels each technician actually evaluated, because API asks about inspection activities, not hours on site. Atlantis also runs ASNT SNT-TC-1A NDT training for the technicians who take the readings; see NDT training in Mobile.

faq.q: Can I take an API 510 class in person in Mobile?
faq.a: There is no Atlantis classroom in Mobile. The API 510 course is self-paced online with instructor Q&A, which lets a candidate from Saraland, Theodore or the Eastern Shore study between shifts without driving to a seminar. The examination itself is in person: once API accepts your application you schedule a seat at a Prometric test centre, sit the closed-book and open-book parts on one day, and API issues the certification to candidates who pass.

faq.q: Does Alabama license the inspectors who work on refinery and chemical plant vessels?
faq.a: The state's Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Act excludes vessels that are part of a manufacturing process, vessels subject to OSHA standards and, under Section 25-12-7(b)(7), pressure vessels associated with oil, gas, refining, chemical, pipeline and storage operations. Inspection of that equipment is therefore run through the owner's mechanical integrity programme, and API 510 certification is the credential employers ask for. The state certificate of competency applies to the power-generation boilers and vessels the statute names.

faq.q: Are hydrocracker reactors like those at Saraland the kind of vessels the API 510 exam covers?
faq.a: Yes, as engineering principles rather than plant facts. The Body of Knowledge includes high-temperature hydrogen attack, high-temperature H2/H2S corrosion and wet H2S damage, and the Section VIII questions about thickness, MAWP and pressure testing apply to heavy-walled reactors as much as to small drums. The exam will not name a refinery. It will expect you to know which materials and conditions make a mechanism likely and which inspection methods RP 571 points to.

faq.q: Which damage mechanisms should an inspector at the McIntosh chlor-alkali plants study first?
faq.a: Start with caustic corrosion, caustic stress corrosion cracking, hydrochloric acid corrosion and chloride stress corrosion cracking, all four of which are on the API 510 list, then corrosion under insulation. Learn the critical factors and appearance of each, which materials are susceptible, and how RP 571 suggests finding them. Remember that only the 15 mechanisms named in the Body of Knowledge are examined, so chlorine-specific topics beyond them will not appear.

faq.q: Is static head on the API 510 exam, and what specific gravity should I use?
faq.a: Yes. The Body of Knowledge lists static head on a vessel part, total pressure at the part and maximum vessel MAWP from part MAWPs and elevations, and it says all static head is based on a specific gravity of 1.0. Use 0.433 psi per foot of liquid above the part, add it to the pressure at the top, and then apply the thickness or MAWP formula for that part.

faq.q: I inspect boilers at a Mobile County power station. Does that experience count toward API 510?
faq.a: Possibly in part, but API 510 experience means supervising or performing inspection of pressure vessels as the code describes, and fired boilers are covered by other rules. Describe any unfired pressure vessels you inspected, such as deaerators, blowdown tanks or heat exchanger shells, separately from boiler work on your application, with dates and your actual duties. API verifies the experience and makes the decision, so precise descriptions help.

faq.q: I have an associate degree from Bishop State. How much inspection experience do I need?
faq.a: If API accepts the degree as a two-year degree or certificate in engineering or technology, you need two years of experience in the design, construction, repair, operation or inspection of pressure vessels, including one year supervising or performing inspection. If it does not, the high school route applies and you need three years. Check the current wording on the certification page before you apply and submit the transcript with your application.

faq.q: Where do Mobile candidates sit the API 510 exam?
faq.a: Prometric lists test centres in and around Mobile, and you choose a centre and seat when you schedule after API approves your application. The examination is delivered on a computer at the centre, with no papers, notes or books allowed. For the open-book part the code documents are provided as PDFs on screen, so practise finding clauses in electronic files rather than in printed books.
